purpose: 60 independently worded original core card answer/marking reviews across all 48 AQA school-mock topic families, including a factual completion of the total-internal-reflection condition.
scope: Actual first-mock Physics AS, taught Chemistry AS/A2 to Kp and organic without buffers, Maths first Year 1 Pure only
edits: Preserve original card IDs and prompts. Keep original backs except the identified TIR definition, which must require both n1>n2 and incident angle greater than critical angle. Guard every patch by exact ID and original text. Curated wrong answers checked before fuzzy marking.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Accuracy vs precision?
records.originalBack: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.
accept: Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value; precision refers to consistency of repeated readings.
reject: Accuracy is the spread between repeated readings and precision measures closeness to the true value.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How is a percentage gradient uncertainty estimated from graph lines?
records.originalBack: |Best gradient − worst acceptable gradient| ÷ |best gradient| × 100%.
accept: Percentage gradient uncertainty is 100 times the difference between best and worst acceptable slope divided by the magnitude of the best slope.
reject: Gradient uncertainty is found by multiplying the worst slope by the best slope.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How do you combine uncertainties when adding or subtracting measurements?
records.originalBack: Add the absolute uncertainties.
accept: For a sum or difference of measured quantities add their absolute uncertainties.
reject: Subtract the absolute uncertainties whenever measurements are subtracted.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: When resolving a vector, what decides whether to use sin or cos?
records.originalBack: Look at the marked angle: adjacent side uses cos θ; opposite side uses sin θ. Never rely on horizontal or vertical.
accept: Use cosine for the component adjacent to the marked angle and sine for the opposite component.
reject: Always use cosine for the horizontal component regardless of the stated angle.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does area below the time axis on an acceleration–time graph mean?
records.originalBack: A negative change in velocity, not a negative distance. It need not mean the object slows down.
accept: Area beneath the axis on an acceleration versus time graph gives negative delta v; it does not necessarily mean slowing down.
reject: Negative area on an acceleration-time plot must represent negative distance travelled.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: On a slope, which way do weight and its two components act?
records.originalBack: Weight mg acts vertically down; mg sin θ acts down the slope; mg cos θ acts into the slope.
accept: Weight acts vertically down; its parallel component mg sin theta goes down the slope and its normal component mg cos theta goes into the slope.
reject: Weight acts perpendicular to the slope rather than vertically down.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Ignoring air resistance, which force acts on a projectile after release?
records.originalBack: Only weight (gravity) acts, vertically downwards; no forward driving force is needed.
accept: After launch and ignoring air resistance, only gravitational force acts on the projectile.
reject: An ideal released projectile needs a constant horizontal driving force to keep moving.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: In the couple formula M = Fd, what does distance d represent?
records.originalBack: d is the perpendicular separation between the forces' lines of action. Use just one F; don't double Fd.
accept: In M=Fd, d is the shortest perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the equal opposite forces.
reject: In a couple, d is the distance travelled by either force during the turn.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Force rises 0→80 N then returns to 0 over 0.20 s. Find impulse.
records.originalBack: Area of triangular F–t graph = ½×0.20×80 = 8.0 N s (change in momentum).
accept: Impulse equals one half times 80 newtons times 0.20 seconds, which is 8.0 N s.
reject: The impulse is 16 N s because the force-time region is a rectangle.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: An object's kinetic energy rises from 5 J to 30 J. What is the net work done on it?
accept: Net work done equals final minus initial kinetic energy, 30 J minus 5 J equals +25 J.
reject: The net work done is negative 25 J because kinetic energy increased.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does gradient of a stress (y) against strain (x) graph give?
records.originalBack: Young modulus E in the linear elastic region: E = stress ÷ strain (in Pa).
accept: The straight-line elastic stress-strain gradient represents Young modulus, measured in pascals.
reject: The gradient of stress against strain has no units because strain has no units.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What phase difference is half a cycle?
records.originalBack: π radians or 180°.
accept: Half a full oscillation corresponds to a phase difference of pi radians or 180 degrees.
reject: A half-cycle phase difference is pi over two radians.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is fringe spacing?
records.originalBack: Distance between adjacent bright fringes or adjacent dark fringes.
accept: Fringe spacing means the separation between successive bright fringes, or between successive dark fringes.
reject: Fringe spacing is always the distance between a bright and neighbouring dark fringe.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How far apart are adjacent stationary-wave nodes?
records.originalBack: Half a wavelength, λ/2.
accept: Consecutive nodes in a stationary wave are separated by lambda divided by two.
reject: Adjacent nodes in a stationary wave are one full wavelength apart.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: When can total internal reflection occur?
records.originalBack: Light travels from higher to lower refractive index.
records.revisedBack: When light travels from higher to lower refractive index AND the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
accept: Total internal reflection needs incidence from a higher refractive index into a lower one at an angle greater than the critical angle.
reject: Light travels from higher to lower refractive index.
The angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why is photoelectric emission effectively immediate above threshold?
records.originalBack: One photon transfers its energy to one electron in one interaction.
accept: With frequency above threshold an individual photon gives its energy to an electron in a single event, so emission has essentially no delay.
reject: Photoelectrons must accumulate energy gradually from many low-frequency photons over a long time.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How does an antiparticle compare with its particle?
records.originalBack: Same mass and rest energy, but opposite charge and other additive quantum numbers.
accept: An antiparticle has the same mass as its corresponding particle but opposite electric charge where charged and opposite additive quantum numbers.
reject: An antiparticle has a smaller rest mass than the corresponding particle.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Which graph is used to find a cell's emf and internal resistance?
records.originalBack: Terminal p.d. V against current I.
accept: Plot terminal potential difference V against current I; y intercept gives emf and negative gradient gives internal resistance.
reject: Plot internal resistance against time to read emf from the slope.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A device receives 150 J and transfers 60 J usefully. Calculate efficiency.
records.originalBack: Efficiency = useful output/input = 60/150 = 0.40 = 40%.
accept: Useful energy divided by input energy is 60 over 150, giving efficiency 0.4 or 40 percent.
reject: Efficiency is 250 percent because input divided by useful output is 150/60.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What causes an optical fibre to guide light?
records.originalBack: Total internal reflection at its boundary.
accept: Fibre light is guided by total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface.
reject: Light is guided because the core repeatedly absorbs and re-emits every photon.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why do isotopes often have similar chemical properties?
records.originalBack: They have the same electron arrangements despite differing neutron numbers.
accept: Isotopes of an element usually react similarly because their electrons are arranged in the same way.
reject: Isotopes of the same element differ in the number of outer-shell electrons.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Write the first ionisation equation for magnesium.
records.originalBack: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻.
accept: Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-.
reject: Mg+(g) -> Mg2+(g) + e- is the first ionisation equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How should percentages be treated when calculating empirical formula?
records.originalBack: Assume a 100 g sample; percentage values become gram masses.
accept: Take a hypothetical 100 g sample so each percentage becomes a mass in grams.
reject: Convert each percentage directly to its atomic number before finding the mole ratio.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: State the complete definition of ionic bonding.
records.originalBack: Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice.
accept: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
reject: Ionic bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between two neutral atoms.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why can graphite conduct along its layers?
records.originalBack: Delocalised electrons move through the layers.
accept: Graphite has mobile delocalised electrons that can carry charge along the carbon layers.
reject: Graphite conducts because whole carbon atoms freely move through the layers.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define enthalpy of atomisation.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms forms from an element in its standard state.
accept: The enthalpy change to form one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.
reject: Atomisation enthalpy is the formation of one mole of liquid atoms from gas.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when an equation is reversed?
records.originalBack: Change the sign.
accept: Reversing the direction of a chemical reaction changes the sign of its enthalpy change.
reject: If a Hess equation is reversed its delta H remains unchanged in sign.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the trend in Group 2 sulfate solubility?
records.originalBack: Solubility decreases down the group.
accept: Group 2 sulfates become less soluble as the group is descended.
reject: Group 2 sulfate solubility rises as the metal gets heavier.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What colour precipitate indicates chloride with silver ions?
records.originalBack: White (AgCl).
accept: AgCl forms a white precipitate with silver ions.
reject: A chloride ion gives a yellow precipitate of silver chloride.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How do you determine units of the rate constant k?
records.originalBack: Rearrange the rate equation and substitute the units of rate and concentration.
accept: Divide the units of rate by the concentration units raised to the powers in the rate law.
reject: Every rate constant has units per second independent of overall order.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: For a graph of ln k against 1/T, what are the gradient and y-intercept?
records.originalBack: Gradient = −Ea/R. y-intercept = ln A. Temperature must be in kelvin.
accept: On ln k plotted against 1/T, the slope is minus Ea over R and the intercept is ln A.
reject: The gradient is positive Ea/R and the y intercept is zero for every reaction.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Does changing total pressure at constant temperature change Kp?
records.originalBack: No. It may change equilibrium position, but Kp itself is unchanged at fixed temperature.
accept: At a fixed temperature changing pressure can alter equilibrium composition but not the value of Kp.
reject: Kp always increases when the total equilibrium pressure is increased at constant temperature.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How is lattice formation enthalpy related to lattice dissociation enthalpy?
records.originalBack: Same magnitude, opposite sign.
accept: Lattice formation and lattice dissociation enthalpies have equal absolute values with opposite signs.
reject: Lattice formation and dissociation enthalpies always have the same sign.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: State the Gibbs free-energy equation and the unit rule.
records.originalBack: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. T in K; use matching energy units for ΔH and TΔS (convert J to kJ if needed).
accept: Delta G equals delta H minus T delta S; T must be in kelvin and entropy and enthalpy must use consistent units.
reject: Delta G equals delta H plus T delta S, and temperature must be in degrees Celsius.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.section: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
records.front: Write the Ka expression for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.
accept: For HA dissociation, Ka is [H+][A-]/[HA].
reject: For HA, Ka equals [HA]/([H+][A-]).

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What bond property makes halogenoalkanes reactive?
records.originalBack: The C–halogen bond is polar.
accept: The carbon-halogen bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative than carbon.
reject: The carbon-halogen bond is nonpolar and therefore attracts nucleophiles.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What group identifies an alcohol?
records.originalBack: Hydroxyl, –OH.
accept: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group, -OH.
reject: The functional group of an alcohol is -COOH.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is required for a common chiral carbon centre?
records.originalBack: Four different substituent groups.
accept: A tetrahedral carbon bearing four distinct substituents is commonly a chiral centre.
reject: A carbon attached to two identical groups is always a chiral centre.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why are carbonyl compounds attacked at carbon?
records.originalBack: Their C=O bond is polar, with carbon δ+.
accept: The carbonyl carbon is partially positive because oxygen attracts the shared bond electrons.
reject: Nucleophiles attack carbonyl carbon because the carbon atom carries a full negative charge.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the reagents and catalyst for esterification?
records.originalBack: A carboxylic acid + alcohol, with concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst and heat/reflux.
accept: React an alcohol with a carboxylic acid using concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst and heating under reflux.
reject: An ester forms by heating an alcohol and a ketone without any catalyst.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What organic product is formed when an acyl chloride reacts with ammonia?
records.originalBack: A primary amide.
accept: Acyl chloride with ammonia gives a primary amide.
reject: Ammonia reacts with an acyl chloride to form an ester.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the main products of triglyceride saponification?
records.originalBack: Soap (long-chain carboxylate salts) and glycerol.
accept: Alkaline triglyceride hydrolysis yields glycerol and salts of long-chain carboxylic acids, called soaps.
reject: Saponification of a triglyceride produces only glycerol and no salts.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why are two burette readings included in uncertainty?
records.originalBack: A titre is a difference; uncertainty arises from both final and initial readings.
accept: A titre uses the difference between a starting and an ending burette reading so both reading uncertainties contribute.
reject: Only the final burette reading contributes uncertainty to a titre.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What functions are inverses of each other?
records.originalBack: y=eˣ and y=ln x.
accept: The exponential y=e^x and natural logarithm y=ln x are inverse functions.
reject: The inverse of y=e^x is y=1/e^x.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the domain of a function?
records.originalBack: Its permitted input values.
accept: The domain is the set of all permitted input values of the function.
reject: The domain is the set of actual output values.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How are gradients of perpendicular non-vertical lines related?
records.originalBack: m₁m₂ = −1.
accept: For two nonvertical perpendicular lines, the product of their gradients is -1.
reject: Two nonvertical perpendicular lines must have equal gradients.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the point–gradient form of a straight-line equation.
records.originalBack: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
accept: y-y1=m(x-x1) for a line of gradient m through (x1,y1).
reject: y-y1=m(x+x1) is always the point-gradient equation.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: When does an infinite geometric series have a finite sum?
records.originalBack: When the common ratio satisfies |r|<1.
accept: An infinite geometric series converges when the magnitude of the common ratio is less than one.
reject: A geometric series has a finite infinite sum whenever r is greater than 1.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the exact value of sin 45°?
accept: The exact value of sin 45 degrees is root two divided by two.
reject: sin 45 degrees equals square root three divided by two.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the exact value of cos 30°?
accept: cos 30 degrees is root three over two.
reject: cos 30 degrees equals one half.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: After using tan⁻¹(y/x) for a vector's angle, what should you check?
records.originalBack: The quadrant, using the signs of both components.
accept: Determine the quadrant from the signs of x and y, then correct the arctangent reference angle.
reject: tan inverse y/x automatically returns the correct full-circle quadrant.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: In which quadrants is sin θ positive?
records.originalBack: Quadrants I and II.
accept: Sine is positive in quadrants one and two.
reject: Sin theta is positive in quadrants three and four.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is logₐ(xᵏ)?
records.originalBack: k logₐx.
accept: log base a of x to power k equals k times log base a of x.
reject: log_a(x^k)=log_a(x)+k.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is logₐ(xy)?
records.originalBack: logₐx + logₐy.
accept: log_a(xy)=log_a(x)+log_a(y) for positive x and y.
reject: log_a(xy)=log_a(x) times log_a(y).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does f′(x)>0 mean over an interval?
records.originalBack: The function is increasing there.
accept: When the first derivative is positive throughout an interval, the function increases there.
reject: If f'(x)>0 then f(x) must be negative throughout that interval.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does a definite integral of f(x) below the x-axis contribute?
records.originalBack: Negative signed area, not automatically positive physical area.
accept: A region below the x axis contributes negative signed area to a definite integral.
reject: A definite integral always counts area under the x-axis as positive.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For total area where a graph crosses the x-axis, what is needed?
records.originalBack: Split at the roots and add the positive areas.
accept: Split the area at x-intercepts, taking absolute values of each signed integral.
reject: Find total area by adding the raw signed integrals even if some are negative.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How do position vectors give the vector from A to B?
records.originalBack: AB = OB − OA (position vectors).
accept: Vector AB is position vector OB minus position vector OA.
reject: AB=OA-OB for all points A and B.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How do you add 2D vectors (a,b) and (c,d)?
records.originalBack: (a+c, b+d).
accept: Add corresponding vector components, giving (a+c,b+d).
reject: The sum is (ac,bd) by multiplying the components.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is k times the vector (a,b)?
records.originalBack: (ka, kb).
accept: Scalar k multiplies both components, giving (ka,kb).
reject: k(a,b)=(a+k,b+k).
